blocks.content: Picture a busy restaurant kitchen during dinner rush.

A waiter takes an order and doesn't personally walk over to the kitchen, the bar, and the dessert counter to tell each one individually and wait for them to confirm. That would be chaos during rush hour.
Instead the waiter clips the ticket onto the order rail and moves on to the next table.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396269868-197211665.png
blocks.alt: A waiter posting a ticket to an order rail, which the kitchen, bar, and dessert station each react to independently

blocks.content: The kitchen sees the ticket and starts cooking. The bar sees it and starts the drink. The dessert station only reacts if there's a dessert on it. The waiter has no idea how many stations will act on that ticket, and honestly, doesn't need to know.

That is event driven architecture in one sentence: services communicate by publishing and reacting to events instead of calling each other directly, and the producer of an event has no idea who, if anyone, is listening.

Compare that to a waiter who has to personally hunt down the chef, the bartender, and the dessert chef for every single order. Add a new station later, like a coffee counter, and now the waiter's routine has to change too. That's the tightly coupled version, and it's exactly the problem event driven architecture avoids.
1. Introduction

In a typical request driven system, Service A calls Service B directly. A knows B exists, knows its address, and waits for a response. If you want a third service, C, to also react to what A just did, you have to go into A and add a call to C.

Event driven architecture flips this around. Instead of Service A calling B and C directly, A just announces "something happened" by publishing an event. Any service that cares can subscribe and react. Services that don't care simply ignore it.

["The producer publishes an event and moves on, it does not wait for consumers to finish anything.","Consumers subscribe to the kinds of events they care about and process them on their own time.","Adding a new consumer never requires touching the producer's code."]
items: The producer publishes an event and moves on, it does not wait for consumers to finish anything.
Consumers subscribe to the kinds of events they care about and process them on their own time.
Adding a new consumer never requires touching the producer's code.

blocks.title: Why this matters for interviews
blocks.content: This pattern shows up constantly in system design interviews once you get past a single service. Whenever the interviewer asks "how do these services stay in sync without calling each other directly", event driven architecture is usually the answer they're fishing for.
2. Events vs commands
Before going further, it helps to separate two words people often use interchangeably: event and command. They sound similar but they shape coupling in opposite directions.
2.1 A command says do something

A command is an instruction aimed at a specific target. "Charge this card." "Reserve this seat." The sender knows exactly who should handle it, and usually expects a direct response back, success or failure.
Commands create coupling on purpose. The caller needs the receiver to exist and to do the thing right now.
2.2 An event says something happened

An event is a fact about the past. "Order placed." "Payment captured." "User signed up." Nobody is being told what to do. The event just states what occurred, and it's broadcast without a specific target in mind.
Whoever is listening can react however they want, or not react at all. The producer doesn't know or care.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396269868-994614406.png
blocks.alt: Order Service sending a command directly to the Payment Service versus publishing an order placed event to an event bus

blocks.content: {"headers":["Event","Command"],"rows":[["States a fact that already happened","Requests an action to happen"],["No specific target, broadcast to whoever subscribes","Aimed at one specific receiver"],["Producer does not expect a reply","Sender usually expects success or failure back"],["Naturally decouples services","Naturally couples sender to receiver"]]}

blocks.title: Naming gives it away
blocks.content: A good habit: name events in past tense, like OrderPlaced or PaymentCaptured. Name commands as imperative verbs, like ChargeCard or ReserveSeat. If your "event" is named CreateInvoice, it's actually a command wearing an event's name.
3. Why event driven architecture decouples services
blocks.text: 3. Why event driven architecture decouples services

blocks.content: Let's make the coupling problem concrete with an e-commerce example. When an order is placed, you need to update inventory, send a confirmation email, and log the purchase for analytics.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396269868-327881172.png
blocks.alt: Order Service making direct calls to Inventory Service, Email Service, and Analytics Service

blocks.content: If Order Service calls each of these directly, it needs to know all three exist, know how to reach them, and handle it if one of them is slow or down. Want to add a fraud check next month? Go modify Order Service again.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396271702-663676264.png
blocks.alt: Order Service publishing one order placed event to an Event Bus, which fans it out to Inventory, Email, and Analytics Services

blocks.content: Now flip it. Order Service publishes a single OrderPlaced event and is done. Inventory, Email, and Analytics all subscribe independently. None of them are visible to Order Service at all.

["The producer does not need to know which or how many consumers exist.","New consumers, like that fraud check, can be added later without touching the producer's code at all.","A consumer that's temporarily down doesn't block the producer or the other consumers."]
items: The producer does not need to know which or how many consumers exist.
New consumers, like that fraud check, can be added later without touching the producer's code at all.
A consumer that's temporarily down doesn't block the producer or the other consumers.

blocks.title: This is the whole point
blocks.content: The value isn't the messaging technology itself, it's that producers and consumers stop needing to know about each other. That's what "decoupled" actually buys you in a growing microservices system.
4. Building blocks
You don't need anything exotic to build this. Three pieces show up in almost every implementation.
4.1 The event bus or message broker
blocks.text: 4.1 The event bus or message broker

blocks.content: This is the middleman that sits between producers and consumers. It receives published events, stores them briefly or durably, and delivers them to whoever has subscribed. Kafka, RabbitMQ, and AWS SNS plus SQS are the usual suspects.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396271704-123152601.png
blocks.alt: A producer publishing to a topic, which delivers the same event to an inventory consumer and an email consumer

blocks.content: 4.2 Topics and queues

Events are usually organized into named channels. Kafka calls these topics, RabbitMQ calls them queues or exchanges depending on setup. A producer publishes to a topic without caring who's subscribed to it, and consumers subscribe to the topics relevant to them.
4.3 Producers and consumers

A producer is any service that publishes events, it never talks to consumers directly. A consumer is any service that subscribes to a topic and processes events as they arrive. The same service can be a producer for some events and a consumer for others.

blocks.title: Broker choice is a detail, not the concept
blocks.content: Whether you use Kafka, RabbitMQ, or SNS plus SQS is an implementation decision. In an interview, it's far more important to explain why you'd decouple these services than to recite broker feature lists.
5. Trade-offs
Event driven architecture isn't free. You're trading immediate, easy to follow calls for something looser and more resilient, and that trade has real costs.
5.1 Eventual consistency instead of immediate

When Order Service calls Inventory Service directly and waits for a response, you know inventory is updated by the time the call returns. With events, Inventory Service updates whenever it gets around to processing the event, a few milliseconds later, or longer if it's backed up.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396271705-823595809.png
blocks.alt: An order placed event at time zero, with inventory, email, and analytics each updating at different, later points in time

blocks.content: For a brief window, different parts of your system disagree about the state of the world. Usually that window is small, but it's never zero, and your design has to accept that.
5.2 Harder to trace a request

A single HTTP request that triggers a chain of direct calls is easy to trace: read the stack, follow the calls. A request that fans out into five independent async consumers is much harder to follow. You need correlation IDs and proper distributed tracing, or debugging becomes guesswork.
5.3 At least once delivery means idempotent consumers
blocks.text: 5.3 At least once delivery means idempotent consumers

blocks.content: Most brokers guarantee at least once delivery, not exactly once. That means the same event can be delivered twice, say the broker retries because it didn't get an acknowledgment in time, even though the consumer actually processed it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396271706-980646755.png
blocks.alt: A consumer receiving a redelivered event, checking whether it was already processed, and skipping duplicate processing

blocks.title: Idempotency is not optional
blocks.content: If your consumer charges a card or reserves the last item in stock, and it isn't idempotent, a single duplicate delivery can double charge a customer or oversell inventory. Always key on something unique, like an order ID or event ID, before doing the actual work.

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Producers and consumers stay independent","State across services is eventually, not immediately, consistent"],["Easy to add new consumers later","Tracing a request across many async consumers is harder"],["A slow or down consumer does not block the producer","Consumers must handle duplicate deliveries safely"],["Natural fit for fanning one action out to many services","More moving infrastructure to operate and monitor"]]}
6. Choreography versus orchestration

Once a single event triggers a chain of steps across multiple services, like placing an order, reserving stock, charging a card, and shipping, you need a way to coordinate that whole workflow. There are two common approaches.
6.1 Choreography: services react to each other
blocks.text: 6.1 Choreography: services react to each other

blocks.content: Each service listens for the event that matters to it and publishes its own event when it's done, without any central coordinator. Order Service publishes OrderPlaced. Inventory Service reacts, reserves stock, and publishes StockReserved. Shipping Service reacts to that, and so on.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396271706-971151211.png
blocks.alt: Order Service publishing order placed, which Inventory reacts to and publishes stock reserved, which Shipping reacts to and publishes shipment created

blocks.content: It's simple to start with because no service owns the whole workflow. The downside is that the overall workflow logic is scattered across every service involved, and it gets hard to answer what happens next without reading through all of them.
6.2 Orchestration: a central coordinator directs the steps
blocks.text: 6.2 Orchestration: a central coordinator directs the steps

blocks.content: A dedicated orchestrator service owns the workflow. It tells Inventory Service to reserve stock, waits for confirmation, tells Payment Service to charge the card, waits, then tells Shipping Service to ship. The individual services don't need to know about each other at all, only about the orchestrator.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396271707-733731356.png
blocks.alt: A central Order Orchestrator directing Inventory Service, Payment Service, and Shipping Service in sequence

blocks.content: This makes the workflow logic visible in one place, which is easier to reason about and modify. The trade off is that the orchestrator becomes a critical piece that everything depends on, and it can turn back into the tightly coupled design you were trying to avoid if you're not careful.

{"headers":["Choreography","Orchestration"],"rows":[["No central coordinator, services react to events","One service owns and directs the whole workflow"],["Simple to start, scales messily as steps grow","Workflow logic stays in one visible place"],["Hard to see the full picture of a workflow","Orchestrator can become a new single point of coupling"],["Good for a handful of independent reactions","Good for workflows with strict ordering or rollback needs"]]}

blocks.title: Pick based on the workflow, not habit
blocks.content: Fanning one event out to independent, unrelated consumers, like inventory, email, and analytics, is a great fit for choreography. A workflow with strict ordering and rollback needs, like a multi step payment flow, often reads more clearly with orchestration.
7. Real world usage and a worked example
blocks.text: 7. Real world usage and a worked example

blocks.content: 7.1 Notification fanout

A common real world pattern is notification fanout: one event triggers several independent notification channels at once, push notification, email, and SMS, each handled by its own consumer subscribed to the same topic. None of them depend on the others succeeding.
7.2 Worked example: an order placed event
blocks.text: 7.2 Worked example: an order placed event

blocks.content: Let's walk through the e-commerce scenario end to end. A customer places an order. Order Service publishes an OrderPlaced event to a topic. Three completely independent services consume it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396271707-635943041.png
blocks.alt: One order placed event consumed independently by Inventory Service, Email Service, and Analytics Service

blocks.title: The scenario
blocks.text: Order Service has no idea Inventory, Email, and Analytics services even exist. It publishes one event and moves on. Each consumer decides for itself what to do with that event and when.

blocks.content: Here is the producer, publishing the event using a Kafka style client:
Notice this function never mentions inventory, email, or analytics. It publishes and returns. Now the inventory consumer, running as a completely separate service:
The email service subscribes to the exact same topic with a different consumer group, so both get their own copy of every event:

blocks.title: Consumer groups matter
blocks.content: In Kafka, each consumer group gets its own copy of every event on a topic. That's exactly why inventory, email, and analytics can all consume the same OrderPlaced event independently without stepping on each other.

Analytics would look almost identical, just logging the order for reporting instead of reserving stock or sending an email. That is the whole trick: one publish call, three independent reactions, zero coupling between them.
8. The interview angle

Event driven architecture rarely shows up as the entire question in a system design interview. It shows up as a piece of a bigger microservices design, usually when the interviewer asks something like "how do these services stay in sync" or "what happens when an order is placed."
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396271708-555343102.png
blocks.alt: A decision point: many independent reactions favor event driven design, a single specific action favors a direct call

blocks.content: ["Mention it when a single action should trigger multiple, unrelated downstream effects, like inventory, email, and analytics all reacting to one order.","Bring up the events versus commands distinction if the interviewer asks how you would name or design the messages.","If the workflow has several steps with strict ordering or needs rollback on failure, mention orchestration by name instead of just waving at \"some coordinator.\"","Always acknowledge the trade-off out loud: eventual consistency and the need for idempotent consumers. Interviewers notice when a candidate treats event driven architecture as a free win instead of a trade."]
items: Mention it when a single action should trigger multiple, unrelated downstream effects, like inventory, email, and analytics all reacting to one order.
Bring up the events versus commands distinction if the interviewer asks how you would name or design the messages.
If the workflow has several steps with strict ordering or needs rollback on failure, mention orchestration by name instead of just waving at "some coordinator."

Always acknowledge the trade-off out loud: eventual consistency and the need for idempotent consumers. Interviewers notice when a candidate treats event driven architecture as a free win instead of a trade.

blocks.title: Do not reach for it everywhere
blocks.content: If Service A just needs a synchronous answer from Service B right now, like checking if a seat is available before confirming a booking, a direct call is simpler and clearer than routing it through a broker. Event driven architecture earns its complexity when you have multiple independent reactions to one thing, not for every service interaction.
